item.research_question: How does varying the mechanical alloying milling time affect the microstructural evolution, phase constitution, contamination levels, and mechanical properties of the Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy prepared by powder metallurgy?
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying in a Fritsch Pulverisette 6 planetary ball mill under high-purity argon (99.9999%) using hardened steel balls (AISI 52100, 15 mm diameter) at 250 RPM with a 10:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio; followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C, 50 MPa uniaxial pressure, 100 °C·min−1 heating rate, and 15 min dwell time.
item.test_conditions: Milling times of 0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 h; sintering of powders milled for 3, 10, 30, and 50 h; microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness (0.2 kgf, 10 s), nanoindentation (100 mN max load), and ultrasound methods.
key_findings: After 10 h of milling, the powder achieves 95 wt.% BCC phase with virtually full homogeneity and no significant segregation.
Carbide formation (ZrC) is detected in sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling.
Oxides (TiO2) are observed in bulks prepared from powders milled for 30 h and 50 h.
The bulk produced from 50 h milled powders exhibits the highest hardness of 675.7 ± 9.8 HV0.2.
The bulk produced from 3 h milled powders exhibits the lowest hardness of 592.9 ± 21.0 HV0.2.
The average grain size of the BCC matrix decreases from 33.8 µm (3 h milling) to 25.2 µm (50 h milling).
Iron contamination increases from undetectable levels to 1.8 at.% (30 h) and 2.2 at.% (50 h) due to milling media wear.
The elastic modulus increases slightly from 134.7 GPa to 138.7 GPa as milling time increases.
item.mechanism: Longer milling times induce severe plastic deformation, reducing powder particle size and creating more refined microstructures in the sintered bulks; this refinement, combined with the Hall–Petch effect and the dispersion strengthening from carbides and oxides formed due to contamination from the steel milling media and graphite dies, leads to increased hardness and elastic modulus.
item.limitations: The method is highly susceptible to contamination, leading to the formation of oxides and carbides even when using controlled atmospheres; prolonged milling increases contamination levels (C, O, Fe) which may negatively impact ductility.
item.future_work: The authors suggest exploiting the formation of oxides/carbides as a way of exploring the oxide dispersed strengthening (ODS) effect, which may play an important role in the strengthening mechanisms of HEAs.
quotes: Ten hours of milling seems sufficient for achieving an optimal equilibrium between microstructural homogeneity and refinement, high hardness and minimal contamination.
Carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling.
The sintered alloy corresponding to 50 h of mechanical alloying exhibits approximately 14% higher hardness than the alloy produced with 3 h of milling.
